div.h2: In this section, we’ll ask some questions about you.
div.p: About you
You’ll need to know:

ul.li: Your Social Security number (SSN) or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
Your Identity Protection (IP) PIN, if the IRS provided you with one
If someone else could claim you as a dependent on their federal tax return

div.p: Fill in your name as it’s written on your Social Security card or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) paperwork. Using a different name could lead to delays in processing your tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What if I changed my legal name last tax year?

modal-content.p: Report your legal name change to the Social Security Administration (SSA), if you haven’t done so already. SSA will update your record and mail you a free replacement card.

The name and Social Security number used on your federal tax return must match what’s on your Social Security card. If they don’t match, there could be delays in processing your tax return and issuing any refunds.

p.strong: What if my name changed since getting my ITIN?

modal-content.p: If you have an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN), report your legal name change to the IRS at the address listed under "Where do I file my Form W-7/W-7(SP)?" in the Form W-7 Instructions.

You’ll need to submit documentation to support your legal name change, such as a copy of your marriage license, divorce certificate, or other official court-related documents validating the name change.

p.strong: Do I need to have the same last name as my spouse in order to file our return jointly?

modal-content.p: No. You and your spouse don’t need to have the same last name. Just make sure that the name you use on your federal tax return matches the name shown on your Social Security card or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) paperwork.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why do we ask for contact information?

modal-content.p: Your mailing address is only used if the IRS needs to contact you or to mail your federal tax refund.
If the IRS needs to contact you, they’ll send you notices by U.S. mail. The IRS only calls by phone in special cases.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why can’t I change the country?

modal-content.p: Currently, Direct File only supports mailing written communications and refunds from the IRS to addresses in the United States.
If you must use an address outside the U.S., you’ll need to file using another product. Learn more about your filing options.

div.h2: Direct File supports only certain citizenship and residency statuses.
div.p: Direct file supports taxpayers who in were U.S. citizens and/or U.S. residents for tax purposes for the entire tax year.

p.a: Learn more about determining tax residency status.

fg-alert.heading: We don’t support all citizenship and residency situations, but other tax services do.

p.a: Find other ways to file your federal taxes.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why do we ask about citizenship?

modal-content.p: Federal income tax responsibilities and procedures can differ depending on whether or not you’re a U.S. citizen.
To ensure you submit the correct tax information, we need to know your citizenship status.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What does it mean to be a U.S. resident?

modal-content.p: A U.S. resident’s income is generally subject to tax in the same manner as a U.S. citizen. Learn about tax residency status.
For tax purposes, you’re a U.S. resident if either of these apply to you:

ul.li: You meet the green card test or the substantial presence test for the calendar year (January 1 – December 31). Review the rules for residency starting dates for these tests to understand when your tax residency began.
You have an active election with the IRS to treat a nonresident spouse as a resident for tax purposes.

modal-content.p: Direct File only supports an election of this kind for taxpayers who in (or before) filed a joint return with an attachment stating their choice to treat the nonresident spouse as a resident for tax purposes.

What if I’m a U.S. resident and a resident of another country?
If you are a resident of both the United States and another country under each country’s tax laws, you are a dual resident taxpayer.

Dual resident taxpayers may be able to claim benefits under an income tax treaty. However, Direct File doesn’t currently support federal tax return filings for dual resident taxpayers. If you are a dual resident taxpayer, you will need to file your federal tax return using another method to claim tax treaty benefits.
To claim treaty benefits as a resident of the other country, you must file a federal tax return using Form 1040NR and attach Form 8833.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: An election to be treated as a resident for tax purposes

modal-content.p: If a nonresident is married to a U.S. citizen or U.S. resident, the spouses can elect to have IRS treat the nonresident spouse as a resident for tax purposes.

Direct File only supports an election of this kind for taxpayers who in (or before) filed a joint return with an attachment stating their choice to treat the nonresident spouse as a resident for tax purposes.

Under this option, IRS treats the nonresident spouse as a resident starting in the tax year in which the spouses first file their choice. In the following years, unless the election has been suspended or ended, IRS will automatically treat the nonresident spouse as a U.S. resident for tax purposes.

p.a: Learn more about a nonresident spouse treated as a U.S. resident.

modal-content.p:
Making the choice
To make this election with the IRS, spouses must attach a signed statement to their joint federal tax return. Direct File doesn’t yet support attachments and can’t be used to file this choice with IRS. To make this choice, find other ways to file your federal taxes.

If spouses have already filed this election
Spouses can use Direct File to file their federal tax return if both of these statements are true:

ul.li: The spouses filed this election with IRS in a past tax year
The election is still active (not suspended or ended)

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What does it mean to be a U.S. national?

modal-content.p: A U.S. national is someone who owes their allegiance to the United States but is not a U.S. citizen. This includes

ul.li: people born on American Samoa and Swains Island
people born of a parent or parents who are non-citizen nationals who meet certain physical presence or residence requirements
certain inhabitants of the Northern Mariana Islands who opted for non-citizen national status.

modal-content.p:
U.S. nationals and taxes
Depending on the situation, a U.S. national may need to file a U.S. tax return only, a territory tax return only, or both. Generally, this depends on whether the person is a bona fide resident of the territory.
Direct File supports people filing a U.S. tax return and may be used by U.S. nationals who are full-year U.S. residents for tax purposes.

p.a: Learn about tax filing for people from U.S. territories.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why am I being asked about states listed in box 15?

modal-content.p: Box 15 on Form W-2 lists states where taxes were withheld.

Sometimes, employers will incorrectly withhold state taxes in the state where their address is, even though you don’t live or work there. If there is a different state listed in box 15 than , you’ll have to file an additional form, which Direct File doesn’t support yet.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Which types of income does Direct File Support?

modal-content.p: Direct file only works if you have certain types of income.
You can use Direct File if you have one or more of these types of income in :

ul.li: Income from an employer (Form W-2)
Unemployment compensation (Form 1099-G)
Social Security benefits (Form SSA-1099)
Distributions for qualified medical expenses from Health Savings Accounts (Form 1099-SA)
Interest income (Form 1099-INT)
Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend
Distributions from employer-sponsored retirement plans, like a 401(k), pension, annuity, 403(b), or governmental 457(b) (Form 1099-R)

modal-content.p: You can’t use Direct File if you had other types of income in . For example:

ul.li: Unreported cash income, such as tips or alimony
Income that’s reported on other tax form, such as gig work

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s a tax household?

modal-content.p: Your tax household may include:

ul.li: If you file a federal tax return for and you can’t be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return
If you and your spouse file a joint return for and your spouse can’t be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return
As long as you claim them on your tax return
Any individuals you could claim, but do not claim as dependents on your tax return

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Can I still use Direct File if someone in my household didn’t have health insurance coverage in ?

modal-content.p: If someone in your household didn’t have health insurance for all of , you can continue filing your federal tax return using Direct File if you meet one of these exceptions:

ul.li: Someone listed you (and your spouse if filing jointly) as dependent(s) on their tax return
Your household income was below $10,000 and you’re filing as Single or Married Filing Separately
Your household income was below $20,000 and you’re filing as Married Filing Jointly, Head of Household, or Qualifying Surviving Spouse

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why can’t I change my SSN?

modal-content.p: You gave the IRS your SSN when you used your ID.me account to sign in to Direct File.
ID.me collected this information from you when you created your account.
You can’t change your SSN in Direct File unless you change your SSN in ID.me first. This helps prevent identity theft.
If you need to change your SSN, contact ID.me, then try signing in to Direct File again.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Where are these work restrictions listed on a Social Security card?

modal-content.p: The Social Security Administration issues 3 types of Social Security cards. All cards include the person’s name and Social Security number.
For people who aren’t U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents, there may be a restriction listed on the front of their Social Security card.
There are 2 types of restrictions:

ul.li: Valid for work only with DHS authorization
Not valid for employment

modal-content.p: For more details, visit the Social Security Administration’s website.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What if my card has a work restriction listed, but it needs to be updated?

modal-content.p: If "Not valid for employment" is printed on your Social Security card and your immigration status has changed so that you’re now a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, ask the Social Security Administration for a new Social Security card.

heading.strong: You can file your federal taxes only as a paper tax return.

Paper returns can take up to 6 weeks to process.
You need an IP PIN to confirm your identity. If you have an IP PIN but can’t find it, you won’t be able to file your tax return electronically.
Try following these instructions to get your IP PIN. Once you have the IP PIN you’re looking for, add it to Direct File.

div.h2: Enter your 6-digit Identity Protection (IP) PIN.

fg-set.question: IP PIN (Required)

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is an Identity Protection (IP) PIN?

modal-content.p: The IRS IP PIN is a 6-digit number assigned to eligible individuals to help prevent the misuse of their Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number on fraudulent federal income tax returns. A new IP PIN will be generated each year.

If the IRS assigned you (or anyone on your tax return) an IP PIN, you must use it to confirm your identity on any return filed during the current calendar year. This includes current year returns as well as any delinquent tax returns.
If you don’t already have an IP PIN, you may get an IP PIN as a proactive step to protect yourself from tax-related identity theft.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why do we ask if you’re blind?

modal-content.p: If you were blind on the last day of , then the standard deduction amount is higher.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: How is blindness defined?

modal-content.p: For tax purposes, you are considered blind if one of these applies:

ul.li: You don’t have any eyesight.
You can’t see better than 20/200 in your better eye with glasses or contact lenses.
Your field of vision is 20 degrees or less.

modal-content.p: Answer Yes to this question if one of these circumstances applies to you at the end of the tax year.
If you aren’t totally blind, you must get a certified statement from an eye doctor stating that one of these is true:

ol.li: You can’t see better than 20/200 in the better eye with glasses or contact lenses.
Your field of vision is 20 degrees or less.

modal-content.p: If your eye condition isn’t likely to improve beyond these limits, the statement should include this fact. Keep the statement in your records. You won’t need to attach it to your federal tax return, but the IRS may need to see it later.

If your vision can be corrected beyond these limits only by contact lenses that you can wear only briefly because of pain, infection, or ulcers, you can take the higher standard deduction for blindness if you otherwise qualify. In that case, select Yes for this question. Otherwise, answer No.
More information is in IRS’s Publication 501.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why do we ask if you’re unable to care for yourself?

modal-content.p: We ask about a person’s ability to care for themselves to figure out if they qualify for certain tax benefits. For example, this information is used to determine if someone is a qualifying person for the Child and Dependent Care Credit (CDCC).
The CDCC is a tax benefit that helps taxpayers who paid for the care of a family or household member while working or looking for work.
As you complete your federal tax return, we’ll ask questions to check if the CDCC applies to you.
Learn more about who is a qualifying person for the CDCC.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Do I need to have records to show I’m unable to care for myself?

modal-content.p: You won’t be asked to send any records with your federal tax return, but the IRS may ask for records later.
If you’re asked for records, you’ll need something that documents the length and nature of the physical or mental condition. For example:

ul.li: A doctor’s note
Medical records or diagnoses
Records of an accident

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s considered full time?

modal-content.p: A full-time student is someone who meets their school’s full-time attendance requirements for 5 months in a calendar year. The 5 months don’t have to be consecutive. Also, the 5 months don’t have to be 5 full months. For example, a student starting a semester mid-January and graduating mid-May attends the school for 5 months.
The student must go to a school with:

ul.li: A regular teaching staff
A course of study
An enrolled student body

modal-content.p: A school includes:

ul.li: High schools
Colleges
Universities
Technical, trade, and mechanical schools
Full-time, on-farm training courses offered through a school or a state, county, or local government agency

modal-content.p: A school doesn’t include:

ul.li: On-the-job training courses
Correspondence schools
Organizations offering only internet courses

modal-dialog.modal-heading: How do I know if I’m someone’s dependent?

modal-content.p: If you relied on someone else (other than your spouse) for support in , they might be able claim you as a dependent on their federal tax return.
There are a few factors that determine whether someone can claim you as a dependent, including:

ul.li: Your relationship to that person
How much they supported you, financially and in other ways
If you lived with them and for how long

modal-content.p: Review Table 5 in IRS Publication 501 to determine if someone else might be able to claim you.
Keep in mind that you aren’t someone else’s dependent if you paid for more than half of your own support (or if your spouse did).

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Who is required to file a federal tax return?

modal-content.p: Not everyone is required to file a federal tax return each year, but it may benefit them to file one anyway.
For U.S. citizens and residents, the question of whether or not they must file a federal tax return depends on their gross income, filing status, and age.
Talk to the person you think could claim you to find out if they’ve got a filing requirement and whether or not they’re filing a return that includes you as a dependent.
